In addition, to accelerate the training process, a pruning mechanism is introduced to construct a truncated objective integration set and a compact candidate pool, thereby reducing computational complex while preserving reliability-critical information. Meanwhile, a hybrid stopping criterion combining uncertainty reduction and estimate stabilization is developed. The performance of the proposed method is illustrated on several examples. Experiment results show that the proposed method can obtain more accurate failure probability estimates with higher efficiency.

title: An active learning method combining Reliability Analysis Transformer and attention-based sampling for high-dimensional reliability analysis
abstract: Reliability analysis faces the challenge of accurately estimating failure probabilities while minimizing the number of time-consuming model evaluations. Surrogate models can significantly alleviate the computational burden. However, the increasing dimensionality of modern engineering systems poses substantial challenges to the performance of traditional surrogate models. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel cross-domain paradigm for high-dimensional reliability analysis, where the dimensionality of random variables is conceptually mapped to the sequence length in natural language processing (NLP). Building on this mapping, a Reliability Analysis Transformer (RAT) is designed to capture complex dependencies between random variables and system responses. Furthermore, based on the principle that similar samples contribute less new information, an attention-based sampling strategy is proposed to measure sample similarity and iteratively select the least similar samples to existing ones from the candidate dataset, thereby improving the accuracy of the RAT. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through four high-dimensional numerical examples and a liquid rocket engine case study. Results show that the proposed method achieves high accuracy and efficiency in handling high-dimensional and large-scale engineering problems.

title: Likelihood-driven reinforcement learning synergizing knowledge graph embedding and supervised pre-training for system-level fault localization
abstract: System-level fault localization remains a critical challenge in vehicle powertrain health management, hindered by complex fault propagation, data scarcity, and the "one/multiple-phenomenon, one/multiple-cause" problem. While data-driven methods excel at component-level diagnosis, their reliance on large annotated datasets and inability to model system topology limit their effectiveness for system-level applications. This paper proposes SPKL-RL, a likelihood-driven reinforcement learning framework that synergizes supervised pre-training with knowledge graph embedding to address these limitations. The framework formulates fault localization as a likelihood optimization within a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). A supervised pre-training module provides a warm-start policy using historical data, mitigating RL's cold-start issue. A knowledge graph embedding module encodes system topology and fault propagation into interpretable vectors. A likelihood-driven mechanism then guides exploration by integrating information gain and knowledge consistency into the reward function. Experimental results on a real powertrain dataset show SPKL-RL achieves 89.3% diagnostic accuracy across 15 fault types, reduces average diagnostic steps from 38 to 16 (58% efficiency gain), and significantly outperforms baselines, particularly in complex cascading (86.9% accuracy) and coupled fault (80.7% accuracy) scenarios. The framework demonstrates substantial advantages in reducing data dependency, improving generalization, and enhancing interpretability for complex system diagnostics.

title: Machine learning-assisted reliability assessment of main girder deflection in suspension bridges
abstract: This study presents a probabilistic reliability assessment method for vertical deflection in long-span suspension bridges, addressing uncertainties and multifactor coupling in deflection prediction. A hybrid model integrating temporal convolutional network (TCN), bidirectional gated recurrent unit (BiGRU), and Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is developed within a unified probabilistic framework. Trained on field data from Nanxi Suspension Bridge using temperature, vehicle load, and historical deflection inputs, the model estimates both the mean and standard deviation of deflections. It achieves a 38.4%–54.4% improvement in point-prediction accuracy and a 3.5%–15.6% increase in interval coverage compared to conventional methods. An extreme-value framework combining the peaks-over-threshold method with a filtered Poisson process is used to fit a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD), with threshold selection guided by diagnostic plots and statistical tests. Convergence toward the generalized extreme value distribution (GEVD) is confirmed. Extrapolation over a 100-year service life and multi-section integration yields a full-span reliability model, identifying critical sections at 2/8l and 6/8l of the main span. The approach offers a theoretically sound and practical tool for life-cycle performance evaluation of bridges under complex environmental and loading conditions.

title: Constraint-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning with adversarial training for resilience enhancement in multi-microgrid voltage control
abstract: The multi-microgrid system faces severe challenges in maintaining voltage stability when subjected to false data injection (FDI) attacks. This paper proposes a constraint-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning (CAMARL) framework, which combines graph neural networks (GNN) to achieve topology-aware state representation, periodic adversarial training, and dynamically adjusted Lagrange multipliers to achieve constraint enforcement. Experiments on IEEE 33-bus, 57-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus systems show that CAMARL consistently achieves the lowest voltage deviation, both in normal conditions and under attack conditions, outperforming multi-agent soft actor–critic, multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient, and five other multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks. Under normal conditions, CAMARL maintains a 99.8% constraint satisfaction rate on the IEEE 33-bus system, the Lagrange penalty mechanism reduces 94.3% of violations compared to the unconstrained benchmark, and keeps the voltage between 0.95–1.05 p.u. Communication resilience analysis indicates that under a full denial-of-service (DoS) attack, 89.2% of constraints are satisfied, and in the worst-case combination of FDI and DoS threats, this proportion is 87.4%. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of components. Removing GNN and the global state sharing module can increase the voltage deviation by up to 433%, and the removal of any single component alone will lead to a 270% performance degradation.

title: Extrapolating optimal selective maintenance strategy in new environments: A meta-reinforcement learning approach
abstract: Selective maintenance, a widely adopted strategy in industry and military fields, has attracted increasing attention over the past decades. It involves selecting a subset of feasible maintenance actions to maximize the success probability of subsequent missions under limited resources. Most existing studies on selective maintenance optimization assume that the system degradation process is known. In many real-world applications, however, when a system is deployed in a new environment, the environmental effects on its degradation process are typically unknown, rendering these methods ineffective. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) approach for extrapolating optimal selective maintenance strategies from known environments to unseen ones. Within the proposed framework, a meta-agent is trained across multiple known environments to acquire generalized decision-making knowledge. When encountering a new environment, the trained meta-agent infers environmental characteristics from collected observations and adapts its strategy accordingly. Furthermore, a data augmentation method is introduced to mitigate performance loss during the initial explorations in new environments. Results from a two-component system and a coal transportation system demonstrate that the optimal selective maintenance strategies vary substantially across environments and highlight the importance of extrapolating adaptive maintenance strategies under unknown environments.

title: Data-Driven break size detection model for small modular reactors based on convolutional neural network-long short-term memory model and SHapley Additive exPlanations
abstract: During a loss of coolant accident (LOCA), timely and accurate detection of the break size is crucial for nuclear power plant safety. However, current methods rely on the personal judgment of operators, which fail to meet the requirements of both speed and accuracy in high-risk situations. In this study, a CNN-LSTM model is proposed to detect the break size of LOCA, with six optimization algorithms used to tune the model hyperparameters. The GWO-WOA optimized model achieves the lowest validation loss (0.1563) and standard deviation (0.01462), outperforming the unoptimized model. To enhance model interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was conducted. Its results align with actual accident analysis, indicating that the model effectively captured the key features of the accident and enhanced the operators' trust in the AI model. Furthermore, three SHAP-based feature selection strategies were analyzed to reduce the number of required features and improve model performance. The results show that the selection strategy based on the mean SHAP value, which reduces the test set MSE from 0.196 (original feature combination) to 0.0396, is closest to the optimal feature combination. These findings offer practical guidance for developing LOCA break size detection systems, enhancing accident response timeliness and effectiveness.

title: Zero-shot cross-domain transfer for remaining useful life prediction of aero-engines via iterative diffusion refinement
abstract: Accurate prediction of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of turbofan engines is critical for effective predictive maintenance. However, conventional models often struggle to generalize when sensor data distributions shift due to variations in operating profiles, environmental conditions, or system configurations. Existing unsupervised domain adaptation methods alleviate this issue by exploiting unlabeled target-domain data, but they still require additional data sampling. In this paper, we present RUL-DiT, a Diffusion Transformer architecture that combines Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models with a Transformer backbone and a novel LSTM-based conditioning network to iteratively refine RUL predictions via diffusion-based posterior denoising. At each reverse-diffusion step, RUL-DiT refines a Gaussian latent posterior whose mean and schedule-defined variance progressively concentrate the RUL estimate, enabling more faithful modeling of gradual degradation processes than conventional models. Crucially, when trained on a single subset of CMAPSS and NCMAPSS, two established benchmark datasets for aircraft engine prognostics, RUL-DiT achieves strong performance relative to previously reported baselines on both datasets. Moreover, RUL-DiT enables zero-shot cross-domain transfer and achieves competitive performance across transfer tasks on several source-target pairs, without requiring any target-domain labels or fine-tuning. This source-only capability enables direct deployment on unseen subsets and engine operating conditions, substantially reducing data collection overhead for RUL prognostics.

title: Intelligent analysis of ship collision accidents via Low-Rank Adaptation-based fine-tuning of medium-scale Large Language Models
abstract: The rapid advancement of intelligent maritime accident analysis requires processing large-scale, multilingual data across wide geographic regions. However, significant challenges remain in objectively constructing Risk Influencing Factors (RIFs) and ensuring accurate information extraction with limited computational resources. To address these gaps, a framework for intelligent analysis of ship collision accidents based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning of medium-scale large language models (LLMs) with limited labeled data was proposed. A bilingual dataset comprising 503 ship collision accident reports was established, and the RIF ontology was derived using a Grounded Theory approach. Using 60 labeled samples, models with ≤ 8 B parameters were fine-tuned, achieving an F1 score of 94.11% on the most challenging accident RIF extraction subtask, surpassing base models by 34.82%. Then, the extracted information was transformed into a 1061-row ×24-column training data matrix via a semantic similarity model, enabling construction of a TAN-BN model. Finally, sensitivity analysis was conducted to identify key RIFs, and case studies were performed to evaluate model performance and validate the proposed framework. The research results showed that the proposed approach advances large-scale, cross-lingual intelligent maritime accident report analysis by improving accuracy and efficiency, reducing computational costs, and supporting reliable safety management decisions.

title: A machine learning-enhanced real-time reliability assessment framework for maritime autonomous surface ships propulsion systems
abstract: Driven by industry-wide digitalization and the pursuit of autonomy, maritime autonomous surface ships (MASS) are transitioning from conceptual design to real-world operation, emerging as a vital future maritime transportation. Among the challenges confronting MASS, the reliability of propulsion systems stands out as a paramount concern due to its direct impact on safety and mission continuity. This study proposes a real-time reliability assessment framework for MASS propulsion systems based on a diagnosis-informed dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN). The framework integrates Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD), Transformer, and Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) models to diagnose faults and update the DBN with real-time evidence, allowing dynamic and adaptive reliability assessment. This approach incorporates real-time fault diagnosis at the component level to refine system-level reliability predictions. The feasibility of the approach was validated using a case study on a diesel-electric hybrid propulsion system using failure rate data and operational data from simulated fault scenarios. The results indicated that the reliability of related subsystems declined significantly, and the hybrid propulsion system dropped to 0.986 on Day 30, after the navigation mission was completed. This framework introduces a causal inference mechanism that bridges the gap between component-level diagnostics and overall reliability assessment, providing a promising approach for intelligent health monitoring and proactive maintenance planning in MASS operations. The results can provide valuable support for decision-making in scheduling, degradation management, and maintenance planning for the MASS propulsion system with actual operation data.

title: Maritime accident severity modeling with operationally realistic multi-factor data-driven bayesian networks
abstract: • Trains and benchmarks TAN, ANB, and expert BNs for severity forecasting • Integrates two-layer geography: named sea regions plus operating locale • Uses multi-state met ocean factors: visibility, wind, sea state, storms, ice • Adds PSC inspection outcomes as a compliance signal in severity modelling • Provides scenario, sensitivity, SoI, and TRI analyses for actionable levers Maritime accident severity analysis supports safety management and emergency preparedness, yet operational realism remains limited in many quantitative models. Common limitations include coarse geographic representation, reduced-granularity met-ocean descriptors, and the omission of Port State Control (PSC) compliance signals. These constraints can mask actionable thresholds and hinder the identification of interpretable, decision-relevant severity pathways. To address this, the study develops Bayesian Network (BN) models to forecast accident severity using a globally distributed, multi-year (2015-2024) dataset of 1050 reports, with granular descriptors of route/region, operating locale, weather, sea-state, visibility, ship profile, human error, and accident type. It assembles a harmonized severity dataset unifying investigation narratives, PSC outcomes, ship registries, and met-ocean validation within a single standardized schema; embeds two-layer geography, multi-state environmental conditions, and compliance signals into one BN severity framework; and benchmarks three BN families, Tree-Augmented Naïve (TAN), Augmented Naïve Bayes (ANB), and a literature/expert topology, on the same dataset. Beyond structure comparison, a unified inference workflow combines Strength-of-Influence, state-wise tornado decomposition, True Risk Influence (TRI), and sequential and simultaneous scenario analysis. All three models were estimated via Expectation–Maximization (EM) and evaluated using stratified 10-fold ROC/AUC. The literature/expert BN achieved the strongest cross-validated discrimination across severity states and was selected for analysis, indicating that structure should be selected empirically rather than assumed a priori. Diagnostic, scenario, and sensitivity analysis show that severity escalates when open-sea operations on dense traffic corridors coincide with adverse environment (storm, poor visibility, rough sea, high winds), human error, and loss-of-control typologies (grounding/capsizing); severity attenuates under benign conditions and contact-type events. Strength-of-Influence results highlight the central roles of route/region→traffic density and weather/visibility→severity pathways. A targeted TRI assessment isolates Accident Type as the dominant lever shifting probability mass into the high-severity state. The findings enable consequence-aware routing and vessel traffic prioritization, type-conditioned emergency preparedness, and human-factor/equipment readiness.

title: Real-time crash risk level prediction of freeways based on a hybrid spatiotemporal deep learning framework with channel redistribution
abstract: The accurate prediction of crash risk from massive traffic data has become a critical challenge for enhancing road safety. To improve real-time crash risk prediction capabilities, a novel hybrid deep learning framework combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Transformers, and STar Aggregate-Redistribute (STAR) Module is proposed (i.e., CNN-Transformer-STAR). Using high-resolution vehicle trajectory data from the NGSIM dataset, the model extracts complex spatiotemporal interaction features to classify the crash risks into three categories: low level, medium level, and high level. Specifically, the CNN branch is employed to capture local spatiotemporal dynamics and cross-feature coupling relationships, while the Transformer models global temporal and spatial dependencies. Additionally, the STAR module implements a centralized scheme to extract a global latent representation, which is then redistributed across feature channels to optimize inter-channel interactions. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a superior AUC of 0.90, outperforming baselines. The transferability of the predictive framework is validated using an external dataset, which shows a good robustness (AUC = 0.86) in different freeway scenarios. The results provide policy guidance for freeway traffic safety management.

title: Hierarchical domain-physical topology enhanced Fully-Connected Spatial-Temporal Graph Neural Network for remaining useful life prediction
abstract: Accurate and reliable Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction is paramount for ensuring the operational reliability and safety of complex industrial systems. However, existing deep learning paradigms often fail to incorporate explicit structural biases derived from physical dependencies, neglecting inherent physical mechanisms and failing to provide rigorous uncertainty quantification. To surmount these challenges, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Domain-Physical Topology Enhanced Fully-Connected Spatial-Temporal Graph Neural Network (HDPT-FC-STGNN). First, to bridge the heterogeneity between symbolic domain knowledge and continuous sensor streams, a Hierarchical Domain-Physical Topology (HDPT) is constructed leveraging high-dimensional semantic embeddings. A hierarchical message-passing mechanism is subsequently devised to explicitly encode topological dependencies, thereby fusing static physical priors with dynamic sensor streams. Second, to mitigate spurious correlations in noise-intensive environments, a Structure-Aware Probabilistic Graph Sampling strategy is introduced. By selectively injecting stochasticity into unreliable data-driven edges, this mechanism treats the graph topology as a latent variable, bolstering the model robustness against epistemic ambiguity. Finally, a Bayesian uncertainty quantification module, governed by a risk-sensitive hybrid loss function, is implemented to yield high-fidelity RUL estimates alongside well-calibrated confidence intervals. Extensive experiments on the C-MAPSS benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both deterministic precision and probabilistic reliability, notably reducing the RMSE by approximately 6.9% on the FD001 subset while ensuring high probabilistic reliability.

title: Knowledge graph-enhanced large language models for explainable causal analysis of crane accidents
abstract: Crane accidents are characterized by high suddenness, chain-like evolution, and strongly coupled causal factors. Traditional experience-driven approaches are insufficient for reliable causal analysis and evidence-grounded interpretation. This study proposes a knowledge graph-enhanced large language model framework for explainable causal analysis and question answering in crane accident scenarios. A domain-specific ontology for crane accident causation is established based on the human-machine-environment-management (HMEM) framework, and a multi-stage automated knowledge extraction pipeline is developed. Using few-shot prompting, relation enrichment, and self-discrimination filtering, the method achieves high-consistency extraction of accident entities and relationships, resulting in a high-quality crane accident knowledge graph. A Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) mechanism is further introduced to integrate BAAI General Embedding (BGE)-based semantic vector retrieval with multi-hop causal path expansion, enabling the retrieval of structurally constrained causal evidence. An evidence-constrained generation strategy ensures that the produced responses are logically coherent, consistent with retrieved causal evidence, and traceable. The CraneSafe QA prototype system supports knowledge extraction, graph visualization, causal chain analysis, and interactive reasoning. Experiments demonstrate improvements in retrieval accuracy, evidence consistency, and noise robustness, with stable performance across queries of varying semantic depth. The results indicate that knowledge graph-enhanced large language models substantially improve the reliability and interpretability of causal analysis in crane accident scenarios.

title: Pump fault diagnosis for vanadium redox flow batteries using an optimized smoothing-based graph convolutional network
abstract: Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRBs) are promising for large-scale energy storage, yet reliable pump fault diagnosis remains challenging due to complex multivariate coupling and limited labeled data. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) provide an effective way to model variable relationships, but their performance is fundamentally limited by the oversmoothing problem, which leads to loss of feature discriminability in deep architectures. To address this issue, an optimized smoothing-based GCN (OS-GCN) framework is proposed. A smoothing factor (SF) is introduced to regulate feature propagation, and particle swarm optimization is employed to determine its optimal value, enabling a balance between information aggregation and feature preservation. Data association graphs for the GCN are constructed based on Euclidean distance (ED) relationships to capture system dynamics. Pump fault data are collected under both controlled and real-world conditions, providing the basis for an in-depth analysis of operating temperature effects, robustness to noise, and the applicability of the proposed model. Experimental results show that OS-GCN significantly outperforms existing fault diagnosis methods under controlled and real-world conditions. These findings confirm that the proposed framework effectively mitigates oversmoothing and improves the accuracy and robustness of VRB pump fault diagnosis.

title: An explicit surrogate model for real-time reliability assessment of face stability in underwater slurry shield tunneling
abstract: Ensuring tunnel face stability in underwater slurry shield tunneling is challenging due to the inherent stochasticity of geotechnical parameters. Despite their advantages, current frameworks face practical limitations: RFM rigorously captures spatial variability, but its computational cost hinders real-time deployment. Conversely, machine learning based RVMs rely on opaque models lacking explicit expressions, restricting their engineering portability. Importantly, groundwater effects are frequently not properly incorporated into existing frameworks. This study proposes a transparent, efficient reliability assessment framework that incorporates groundwater via the effective stress principle and the upper-bound theorem of limit analysis. A high-fidelity dataset of 4000 samples, accounting for parameter cross-correlations, is used to train a Back-Propagation Neural Network (BPNN). By extracting an explicit algebraic expression from the network, the framework eliminates model opacity and platform dependency. Combined with Sobol sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations, this surrogate model facilitates real-time determination of reliability-based face support pressure. Results indicate that the reliability-based surrogate model achieves an instantaneous execution time of 0.3 s, marking a substantial acceleration from the 55 h required by the traditional RFM. Moreover, it yields more conservative design values, thereby providing an additional safety buffer for engineering applications. Field validation at the Jiangyin-Jingjiang Yangtze River Tunnel confirms the framework's practical utility for real-time safety assessment in sandy strata.

title: Deep reinforcement learning-driven resilience optimization for infrastructure systems: A socio-technical perspective integrating functional resonance analysis method
abstract: Escalating natural disasters and growing infrastructure complexity render resilience optimization indispensable for sustaining operations and mitigating losses. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offers powerful optimization potential, current models often overlook the interactions and variability inherent in socio-technical systems. Integrating DRL with the functional resonance analysis method (FRAM) shows promise, yet remains impractical without a dedicated focus on resilience-oriented controls. Accordingly, this paper proposes a FRAM-DRL framework tailored for infrastructure resilience optimization. Its key advancements are threefold: (1) extending FRAM into a multi-stage structure to capture socio-technical features throughout the resilience lifecycle; (2) establishing variability analysis rules to transform qualitative FRAM into an interactive environment; and (3) defining FRAM-based state, action, and reward representations to facilitate DRL training. The framework was applied to urban metro system (UMS) resilience under extreme rainfall, leveraging the Nanjing Metro case. Results demonstrate that the Dueling DQN performed best among the tested value-based architectures, with action constraint (κ=4) providing the optimal balance between optimization gain and cost efficiency. The learned policies prioritize high-leverage domains and early-stage controls, achieving a favorable reward-efficiency advantage over heuristic strategies via global policy search. Overall, this work methodologically advances Safety-II-oriented proactive management, offering a transferable basis for broader resilience research.

title: AL-IDNN: Active learning method based on incremental updating of deep neural networks for structural reliability analysis
abstract: Reliability analysis is essential for ensuring the safety of engineering systems under uncertainty. In reliability analysis, surrogate models are widely used to reduce computational cost. However, improving the accuracy of reliability analysis typically requires the continuous introduction of critical samples and repeated reconstruction of the surrogate model. To improve model accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency, this paper proposes an active learning method for structural reliability analysis based on incremental updating of deep neural networks (AL-IDNN). The proposed method preserves the knowledge learned by the existing model through parameter inheritance, thereby eliminating the need to retrain the model from scratch. Meanwhile, an adaptive sampling strategy is employed to enrich the design of experiments (DOEs). By combining model predictions with the distribution characteristics of the sample space, critical samples near the limit state surface (LSS) are identified. Furthermore, the DOEs updating strategy is introduced to control sample quality and improve the fitting accuracy to the LSS. Comparative studies with similar methods are conducted to evaluate the proposed AL-IDNN method. Results from benchmark examples and a prestressed hollow slab girder bridge case demonstrate its effectiveness in terms of both accuracy and efficiency in reliability analysis.

title: Decision reliability analysis framework for intelligent unmanned system-of-systems using the cooperative multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient
abstract: The decision reliability is the capability of the intelligent unmanned system-of-systems (IUSoS) to make and execute decisions under a disturbed environment. However, the inherent uncertainty of individual autonomy may render decisions unreliable, leading to task failures and resource wastage. To address this issue, we propose a novel decision reliability analysis framework for the IUSoS using the cooperative multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (C-MADDPG). Firstly, considering individual autonomy and functional diversity, a multilayer operation network based on graph coloring theory is established to provide a foundation for decision analysis. Secondly, a distributed decision model based on the enhanced actor-critic (AC) architecture is presented to maintain the individual stable decision-making ability. Thirdly, considering the impact of individual decisions on reliability, an operation-loop-oriented decision reliability assessment model is proposed to quantify decision reliability. Then, the decision reliability is optimized by the C-MADDPG algorithm, which updates the enhanced AC network with the cooperative reward. Finally, a case study on a multi-agent collaborative scenario demonstrates the feasibility of the methodology. The proposed method receives the most rewards compared with variant algorithms and consistently outperforms them in task completion degree, providing a technical approach for improving system-of-systems reliability under distributed architectures and demonstrating that the cooperative reward mechanism balances individual autonomy with system reliability.

title: Cascading failure analysis of critical infrastructure in conflict zones: a large language model-driven knowledge graph framework
abstract: Modern geopolitical conflicts increasingly target interdependent critical infrastructures, where localized damage can trigger cascading failures, leading to widespread disruption of essential public services. Traditional intelligence safety assessment frameworks struggle to process the dynamic, unstructured data streams from conflict environments. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a novel probabilistic framework for dynamic cascading failure analysis of Critical Infrastructure (CI) under attacks by integrating Large Language Model (LLM) and Knowledge Graph (KG). Our novel dual-graph architecture first employs an LLM to automatically construct a Dynamic Battlefield Event Knowledge Graph (BEKG) from real-time Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), capturing tactical events as they unfold. This dynamic event layer then serves as evidence for a probabilistic inference process on a static Infrastructure Service Dependency Knowledge Graph (ISDKG), which is modeled as a Bayesian Network (BN). This integration enables the simulation of the propagation of cascading failures, translating initial physical damage into a quantifiable risk assessment of widespread service disruptions. Validated through a case study on Ukraine's infrastructure, our system demonstrates high fidelity in automated knowledge construction, provides novel insights into cascading impact analysis, and offers a powerful decision-support tool for assessing the systemic vulnerability and resilience of complex infrastructure networks in conflict zones.

title: Mitigation action-dependent prediction of nuclear plant parameters for severe accident management via conditional generative model
abstract: Effective severe accident management in nuclear power plants requires situational awareness to anticipate multivariate plant responses under time pressure and uncertainty. While artificial intelligence–based surrogate models can support real-time decisions, many studies use recursive multistep forecasting, which tends to accumulate errors over long horizons and often does not reflect operator mitigation actions explicitly. This study proposes an action-conditioned, multivariate multistep prediction model for severe accident decision support. By integrating a transformer, Autoformer, temporal convolutional network, and conditional variational autoencoder, the model produces direct multi-horizon forecasts with uncertainty estimates and represents mitigation actuation states as conditional inputs. For model training and testing, a database was generated using the MAAP 5.06 code with optimized discretization intervals used for data generation and Latin hypercube sampling applied to obtain representative severe accident scenarios with reduced computational cost. The resulting action-conditioned predictions support technical support center staff and plant operators in comparing mitigation options against a no-action baseline and also in assessing key safety-related trends during severe accident progression.

title: Robust reinforcement learning with graph neural networks for stochastic urban rail daily maintenance scheduling
abstract: Urban rail daily maintenance scheduling is challenged by urgent task insertions, limited time windows, and multi-resource requirements. This paper formulates the problem as a stochastic resource-constrained project scheduling problem on dynamic directed acyclic graphs and proposes a preference-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) and deep reinforcement learning framework for real-time rescheduling. The GNN combines precedence-aware propagation and change-decaying message passing to encode topology shifts after interruptions and insertions, while deterministic action masking guarantees precedence- and resource-feasible decisions. The policy is conditioned on a dispatcher-specified preference vector and trained with an Augmented Tchebycheff objective, enabling online adaptation among makespan, overtime penalty, financial cost, maintenance quality, and resource fairness without retraining. Experiments on PSPLIB show near-optimal static performance, including a 0.29% optimality gap on J120 with linear inference complexity. In stochastic insertion environments, the method achieves strong Pareto-front quality in hypervolume, IGD, and non-dominated solutions, while obtaining the best fixed-preference composite cost with sub-second inference latency. It also demonstrates robust cross-scale and zero-shot transfer to the Shenzhen Metro network. On real-world metro data, the framework achieves an average makespan of 625.03 min in 1.17 s, while additional stress tests verify its robustness, interpretability, and industrial applicability.

title: Dynamic vulnerability assessment of urban rail transit systems using spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: A dynamic vulnerability assessment framework that integrates deep learning and complex networks is proposed to better understand the responses of urban rail transit (URT) systems to various disruptions. Specifically, a spatiotemporal deep learning model is developed to forecast network passenger flows over different time periods. A node importance evaluation method considering dynamic travel demands and static network structural characteristics is presented. A comprehensive metric is designed to assess both structural and functional vulnerabilities of the network. The proposed method is validated using Shanghai's URT system as a case study. The results reveal that: (1) The proposed graph convolutional network-temporal kolmogorov-arnold network (GCN-TKAN) model accurately predicts passenger flows across different time periods, achieving an average R² of 0.865 on the testing data, an improvement of 0.056 compared to the second-best model (TKAN); (2) When a sequential single-node attack, guided by the proposed node-importance metric, removes the top 5% of stations, overall network performance drops by 45.00%, which is 4.92% higher than the average decline caused by other basic attack strategies. The innovation of this study lies in the joint modeling of time-varying passenger flows and spatial topological properties, which accurately quantifies the network's vulnerability under different disturbance scenarios, providing a theoretical basis for enhancing system resilience.

title: An adaptive multi-dimensional protection framework for 5G cloud-native networks using collaborative multi-agent systems
abstract: With the deep integration of cloud infrastructure and 5G, microservices have become the mainstream architecture for operators to deliver core network services to 5G users. However, the fine-grained nature of such services also expands the attack surface, introducing new security risks. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a dynamic security policy configuration framework for microservices. Based on the Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) algorithm, the framework resolves high-dimensional collaborative decision-making problems in microservice scenarios through cooperative gaming and state sharing among intelligent agents. Compared with existing static or single-agent solutions, our framework enables more efficient security collaboration in multi-agent environments. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the framework can dynamically formulate security protection and quality of service (QoS) assurance strategies according to the current system state, thereby effectively resisting continuous adversarial attacks while minimizing the impact on service quality.

title: Active Bayesian support vector regression with importance sampling for rare event reliability analysis
abstract: Importance sampling achieves variance reduction by introducing an importance sampling density function, and it is one of the most promising methods for reliability analysis. This paper aims to further improve the efficiency and accuracy of importance sampling by integrating the Bayesian support vector regression model with an active learning strategy, thereby enabling its application to a broad spectrum of engineering problems involving rare event analysis. To achieve this, we propose a novel learning function and a new candidate samples construction method that allow the model to actively select training points near the failure surface, characterized by the highest prediction error and greatest spatial diversity. Additionally, we introduce a stopping criterion based on the global prediction error across unclassified points, ensuring that the algorithm terminates with sufficient accuracy. Through both academic case studies and practical engineering examples, we demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms traditional importance sampling methods as well as other active learning surrogate modeling techniques in terms of efficiency and accuracy.

title: Optimization of risk-based and cost-minimized maintenance strategy for corroded pipeline using reinforcement learning
abstract: This study proposes an innovative reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach for long-term maintenance planning in multi-zone pipeline systems. The RL-based model aims to optimize maintenance decisions by minimizing total life-cycle cost. A modified Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) was first developed to predict corrosion depth and length. Failure probabilities before and after repair were then calculated. The Dueling Deep Q-Network (Dueling DQN) model was employed to find an optimal, zone-specific maintenance strategy. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis was also conducted to evaluate the impact of key parameters, including consequence cost, failure probability threshold, composite repair effectiveness and operating pressure. Case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the RL model in providing an adaptive and efficient approach to pipeline maintenance under corrosion growth uncertainty. Higher consequence costs and stricter failure probability thresholds lead to earlier interventions, while weaker repair effectiveness causes the model to schedule more frequent maintenance actions. Higher operating pressure significantly increases failure risk and total cost. Under extremely high operating pressure, using replacement at the beginning provides greater long-term benefits than using composite wrap. This study provides a framework for data-driven, risk-based maintenance decision-making in complex pipeline systems.

title: Cross scenarios interpretable quantification of maintenance action effects on system health via liquid Kolmogorov–Arnold operator based framework
abstract: Predictive maintenance for safety–critical assets demands accurate forecasting and interpretable understanding of how maintenance actions affect system health across diverse regimes. We introduce a liquid Kolmogorov–Arnold operator (KAO)-based model that learns a physically grounded health indicator (HI) while revealing maintenance-driven degradation dynamics. The model comprises three components: (i) a BoltzmannKAN attention layer learning per-channel thresholds and temperatures to identify key sensors before and after maintenance; (ii) a self-organizing pool of interpretable operators representing distinct degradation modes, connected via liquid, temperature-controlled soft routing for smooth regime transitions; and (iii) unsupervised contrastive learning around maintenance events anchoring the HI without remaining useful life (RUL) labels, guided by a unified loss combining reconstruction, maintenance-quality classification, and regularization terms. The liquid-KAO framework generates a forward-looking HI reflecting both short-term recovery and long-term degradation moderation, while its autoregressive design enables post-maintenance forecasting and counterfactual analysis. On C-MAPSS with simulated interventions, it provides stable forecasts and identifies mechanism shifts consistent with injected actions; on the real-world National General Aviation Flight Information Database (NGAFID) aircraft maintenance dataset (14 maintenance classes), it achieves 0.84 accuracy, surpassing prior baselines with subsystem-level interpretability and HI-based reliability metrics. Overall, liquid-KAO unifies accuracy, transferability, and equation-level interpretability for reliable maintenance validation and scheduling.

title: A novel data-driven quantitative resilience evaluation method for large-scale systems
abstract: To address disaster-induced damages to systems, resilience theory offers a broader and more practical alternative to traditional risk theory. However, resilience evaluation for large-scale systems faces challenges such as massive data and complex disaster scenarios. This paper proposes a data-driven framework for large-scale system resilience evaluation. First, a standardized dataset structure is defined, and a disaster process recognition method based on metric learning is developed. Second, probabilistic functions linking disaster processes to system performance are established as resilience indicators. Third, a data reduction framework is introduced to mitigate issues of excessive data volume and redundant features by reducing both features and attribute values, thus improving recognition accuracy and reducing storage requirements. Finally, case studies on wind power installations under extreme cold and typhoon threats in two regions of China are conducted. Results show that the average deviation between resilience evaluations based on reduced data and full data is within 5%, while data storage is reduced by 35.8%. This provides data-driven decision support for wind farm managers and alleviates challenges posed by large data volumes.

title: The price of decentralization in managing engineering systems through multi-agent reinforcement learning
abstract: Inspection and maintenance (I&M) planning involves sequential decision making under uncertainties and incomplete information, and can be modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). While single-agent deep reinforcement learning provides approximate solutions to POMDPs, it does not scale well in multi-component systems. Scalability can be achieved through multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), which decentralizes decision-making across multiple agents, locally controlling individual components. However, this decentralization can induce cooperation pathologies that degrade the optimality of the learned policies. To examine these effects in I&M planning, we introduce a set of deteriorating systems in which redundancy is varied systematically. These benchmark environments are designed such that computation of centralized (near-)optimal policies remains tractable, enabling direct comparison of solution methods. We implement and benchmark a broad set of MADRL algorithms spanning fully centralized and decentralized training paradigms, from value-factorization to actor-critic methods. Our results show a clear effect of redundancy on coordination: MADRL algorithms achieve near-optimal performance in series-like settings, whereas increasing redundancy amplifies coordination challenges and can lead to optimality losses. Nonetheless, decentralized agents learn structured policies that consistently outperform optimized heuristic baselines, highlighting both the promise and current limitations of decentralized learning for scalable maintenance planning.
keywords: Decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes

title: OceanPathRL: Deep reinforcement learning-based energy-efficient route optimization system for autonomous electric vessels
abstract: Autonomous electric vessels operating in complex maritime environments must simultaneously optimize energy consumption, maintain regulatory compliance, and coordinate with multiple vessels in real time, yet no existing framework addresses all three objectives within a unified learning architecture. This paper presents OceanPathRL, a novel deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-efficient route optimization in autonomous electric vessels. We propose a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture that integrates Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) with attention-based neural networks and a COLREGs-compliant reward formulation to enable real-time path planning under dynamic ocean conditions, including wave energy prediction and photovoltaic uncertainty management. Extensive evaluations on two publicly available benchmarks, namely the Singapore Maritime Dataset and the MarineCadastre AIS dataset, demonstrate that OceanPathRL achieves a 34.7% reduction in energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a 99.2% collision avoidance success rate and 98.0% COLREGs compliance across head-on, crossing, overtaking, and multi-vessel encounter scenarios. The proposed meta-learning transfer mechanism reduces adaptation steps to new maritime environments by approximately 72.8% relative to conventional training, corresponding to a 3.68× average speedup. These results establish OceanPathRL as a practical and scalable solution for next-generation autonomous maritime systems, directly contributing to the International Maritime Organization decarbonization targets and advancing the field toward deployable, regulation-aware autonomous navigation.

title: Causal Contrastive Learning for Reliability-oriented Fault Detection in Wastewater Treatment under Process Uncertainty
abstract: To ensure reliable operations and quality control in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), data-driven fault detection has received wide attention recently, but reliable detection of faults or failures with respect to process variables or quality-related variables remains challenging due to significant process uncertainty. In WWTPs, fault detection is usually affected by data uncertainty, operating-condition uncertainty, and inter-variable relationship uncertainty. These uncertainties are essentially caused by delayed water-quality measurements, wastewater influent loads, or other environmental factors, such as temperature and humidity. In response to these issues, this study proposes causal structure contrastive learning (CSCL) for reliable WWTPs fault detection. In this method, CSCL addresses observation uncertainty by learning window-level representations rather than relying on isolated delayed measurements. Also, it can handle operating-condition uncertainty through causality-preserving augmentation, which retains normal causal structures under admissible influent and process variations. Furthermore, inter-variable relationship uncertainty, by constructing causality-disrupted negative samples that break internal causal dependencies or perturb exogenous-disturbance-driven causal patterns, can be addressed efficiently. By comparing causality-consistent with causality-disrupted samples, CSCL can separate normal process variability from fault-induced causal changes, thereby strengthening the reliability of fault detection. Experiments on BSM2 fault scenarios and full-scale WWTP data demonstrate that CSCL can outperform other fault detection baselines.

title: Neural Scheduling for Carrier Aircraft Recovery with Bolter and Aerial Refueling
abstract: Existing carrier aircraft recovery scheduling studies commonly assume a predetermined aircraft set, limiting their applicability to safety-critical operations involving bolter events, fuel-endurance risk, and online insertion of new-wave tasks. This study formulates dynamic carrier aircraft recovery scheduling as an event-driven sequential decision-making problem that jointly considers bolter recovery, aerial refueling, remaining-fuel evolution, and online task insertion. A Long-Range Dependency-Aware Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm, termed LDA-PPO, is developed by integrating a dynamic recovery pool with a multi-layer masking mechanism. The pool maps time-varying aircraft sets to a stable neural decision interface. The dynamic-recovery-pool and attention masks exclude empty slots from representation learning, while the action-feasibility mask excludes unavailable aircraft from action selection. Each aircraft is encoded as an aircraft token, and multi-head self-attention captures global dependencies in fuel safety, mechanical integrity, mission priority, bolter risk, and new-wave arrivals. In 128 single-wave scenarios with 32 aircraft, LDA-PPO combined higher mean composite objectives and low online computational cost with fewer touchdown fuel-reserve violations and better fuel reliability than most baselines. It handled different task sizes within the dynamic recovery pool capacity and multi-wave missions without parameter updates. The proposed method provides a reliability-oriented online decision-support framework for dynamic carrier aircraft recovery.

title: Pseudo-Anomaly Data Driven Robust and Confidence Information Redundancy Approach in Aircraft Components
abstract: Information redundancy (IR) for flight parameters requires robustness to corrupted auxiliary measurements and confidence assessment of the resulting estimates. This paper proposes a Pseudo-Anomaly data-driven Robust and Confidence IR (PA-RCIR) framework. A Random Anomaly Scenario Generator (RASG) generates pseudo-anomalous auxiliary inputs through complementary signal-level perturbations while preserving their target references. A Dual-phase Robust Variational Inference Network (DRVIN) jointly learns from original and perturbed inputs using a probabilistic latent representation. An Empirical Cumulative Distribution function of prediction Statistical Features (ECDSF) constructs empirical confidence scores from repeated prediction samples and a normal-validation reference distribution. Experiments use real flight records from the Thor and Ibis UAV datasets, with angle-of-attack (AoA) redundancy as a representative task and separate training and evaluation on each dataset. Over ten runs, the mean absolute error (MAE) under normal inputs is 0.0120 on Thor and 0.0007 on Ibis. Under controlled bias and noise corruptions affecting five auxiliary-input channels, the corresponding values are 0.0200 and 0.0012. In both evaluated multichannel mixed-anomaly scenarios, PA-RCIR achieves statistically significant improvements over all six baselines for the three prediction-error metrics after Holm correction. Representative cases and expected calibration error analysis characterize the relationship between confidence scores and prediction quality, with calibration behavior varying across input conditions and prediction-sample statistics. These results support robust information redundancy with empirical confidence assessment under the evaluated input conditions.

title: Context-Aware Prompt Encoding Compression and Sentence-Level Pooling based LLMs for Industrial Equipment Health Status Prediction
abstract: Accurate forecasting of industrial equipment health states is crucial for improving system reliability, enabling predictive maintenance, and supporting intelligent manufacturing. Conventional forecasting methods primarily rely on structured sensor data and often fail to leverage reliability-related knowledge contained in unstructured sources such as maintenance reports and failure logs. Although large language models (LLMs) show strong capabilities in textual understanding, their application to industrial prognostics and health management remains limited due to weak integration with quantitative signals and sensitivity to irrelevant textual information. To address these issues, this study proposes a cross-modal forecasting framework, Context-Aware Prompt Encoding Compression and Sentence-Level Pooling–Large Language Model (CASP-LLM). The framework integrates maintenance text with sensor time-series data to improve equipment health-state prediction. Prompts derived from statistical characteristics of sensor signals guide context-aware encoding and sentence-level pooling to extract reliability-relevant semantic features, while a parallel pathway captures temporal degradation patterns from sensor observations. The resulting representations are fused for prediction. Experiments are conducted on public fuel cell datasets and two real industrial heat exchanger datasets. The results demonstrate that CASP-LLM consistently outperforms LSTM, Transformer, TimeLLM, and other comparative models across multiple forecasting horizons.

title: Uncertainty-aware dynamic-static knowledge injection for few-shot electromagnetic interference failure assessment via large language models
abstract: Electromagnetic interference (EMI) can reduce the reliability of electronic systems and lead to functional failures, making EMI immunity assessment essential for reliable system operation. However, such assessment usually requires many experiments, and the resulting data are often costly or unavailable. This makes few-shot EMI failure assessment difficult, especially when model uncertainty must be controlled and physical constraints must be respected. To address the above issues, we propose the Dynamic-Static Knowledge Injection Large Language Model (DSKI-LLM) for few-shot EMI failure assessment. The framework contains a static knowledge injection module and an uncertainty-aware dynamic module. The static module combines Domain-Corrective Alignment Loss with gated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to encourage representations consistent with electromagnetic knowledge. The dynamic module uses predictive entropy to estimate confidence and adjusts retrieval depth during inference. Low-confidence queries retrieve more historical EMI cases, while high-confidence queries avoid unnecessary context expansion. We evaluate DSKI-LLM on PhyEMI, a benchmark dataset built from a controlled EMI experimental platform. Results show that DSKI-LLM improves few-shot prediction over the evaluated baselines and produces more reliable probability estimates. By combining prediction with uncertainty estimation and adaptive evidence retrieval, the proposed method supports more trustworthy EMI failure assessment under limited data.

title: AI-Enabled construction safety management: A paradigm shift from passive compliance to proactive empowerment
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to construction safety through hazard recognition, risk assessment, monitoring, and decision support. Despite rapid advances, existing systems differ substantially in their ability to interpret risk, generate safety-related outputs, and assume intervention authority. This study develops a reliability-oriented maturity framework to classify AI-enabled construction-safety functions. A PRISMA-guided review identified 171 eligible publications, including 153 technical studies and 18 reviews. The technical studies were characterized using two complementary dimensions: Objective Scanning Response (OSR), describing risk-information processing, and Safety State Output (SSO), describing safety-related output. Building on these functional profiles, an L0-L5 maturity framework is developed to characterize functional position, intervention authority, Operational Design Domain, and fallback capability. A Perception-Cognition-Decision-Execution (P-C-D-E) architecture is further developed to represent the functional structure of closed-loop safety intervention, including fast-slow functional separation, state verification, and fallback. Representative scenarios illustrate the framework’s application. The coded evidence indicates a marked asymmetry between risk understanding and physical intervention. The framework remains theoretically derived and has not undergone independent maturity-classification validation. Its contribution is nonetheless substantive: it provides a reproducible classification procedure, an authority-allocation model, and a reliability-oriented evaluation pathway specifying the evidence required before higher levels of autonomous intervention can be justified.

title: Sparse stage path graph Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for bearing remaining useful life prediction
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been utilized to analyze monitoring data for predicting the remaining useful life (RUL) of bearings. Conventional methods typically aggregate degradation features through GNNs after converting the monitoring data into graphs. However, traditional GNNs face two primary challenges: (1) a single stage of graph data construction is insufficient to capture the complexity of bearing degradation, and (2) the effectiveness of these methods heavily depends on the selection of initial weights, making them susceptible to noise interference. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel sparse stage path graph Kolmogorov-Arnold network (SSPGKAN) model to enhance bearing RUL prediction. First, a siamese KAN model is developed to classify bearing degradation stages, and stage path graphs (SPGs) are constructed to aggregate the degradation features. Subsequently, the SSPGKAN model replaces traditional edges in the graph structure with learnable functions, overcoming the limitations of initial linear weight selection in GNNs and enabling dynamic transmission of graph data. Additionally, a sparse graph optimization method is used to reduce the impact of noise and accurately predict bearing RUL. Verification results from two test bench datasets demonstrate that the SSPGKAN model improves the prediction efficiency and accuracy of bearing RUL.

title: Resilience enhancement study of renewable energy power networks by integrating subnet division and priority enhanced Q-Learning
abstract: With the acceleration of global energy transition and escalating climate challenges, the large-scale integration of renewable energy into power systems has become inevitable. However, the intermittency of renewable energy output significantly exacerbates the risk of cascading failures in power grids. Traditional critical node protection and post-fault restoration methods struggle to adapt to renewable energy uncertainties, bottlenecking grid resilience assessment and enhancement. This study proposes a dual-phase resilience enhancement framework for renewable energy power systems, addressing pre-failure protection and post-failure restoration challenges. The methodology integrates a Subnet Division-Based Strategy and a Priority Enhanced Q-Learning-Based Restoration to mitigate cascading failures. Subnet Division-Based Strategy partitions networks into functional subnets using breadth-first search and maximum flow algorithms, identifying critical nodes through betweenness centrality optimization. Priority Enhanced Q-Learning-Based Restoration incorporates subnet priority rankings into Q-learning to create a guided exploration mechanism for repair sequence optimization. Experimental validations on IEEE test cases with renewable energy show that: 1) The Subnetwork Division-Based Strategy enables critical node protection, reducing resilience loss by 10%–30% across four attack scenarios; 2) Priority Enhanced Q-Learning-Based Restoration achieves 10% lower resilience loss and a 0.5–1 unit resilience improvement compared to conventional methods; 3) Subnet division prioritization combined with Q-Learning yields a 26.3% performance gain. This dual-phase approach provides grid operators with preventive protection strategies and real-time restoration optimization capabilities, establishes a replicable framework for enhancing network resilience.

title: A GCN-based availability analysis method for mobile network with spatial–temporal effect awareness
abstract: The spatial–temporal effect induces complex dynamic changes in the states of network, increasing the risk of mobile network unavailability. Current availability analysis methods are difficult to establish the network spatial–temporal dynamic variation pattern. Machine learning methods avoid the weakness of explicitly modeling effect patterns. However, these methods usually neglect spatial topology changes and abrupt temporal dynamics. To address the above problem, we propose a GCN-Based Availability Analysis Method for Networks with Spatial–Temporal Effect Awareness (Gstea). In the spatial domain, the spatial variation is captured by graph adaptation and graph convolution. In the temporal domain, the Ek (ERP-based time-aligned with k-shape integration to preserve shape similarity) fully aligns the temporal sequence to identify abrupt network changes and generates enhanced graph signal propagation. Experimental results show that Gstea outperforms the best-performing baseline methods in various complex network scenarios (average improvement range from 7% to 26%). This demonstrates that Gstea can provide a more accurate evaluation in networks with spatial–temporal effect.

title: An interpretable fault diagnosis framework for nuclear power plant via graph representation and multi-task learning
abstract: Neural networks have great potential for enhancing fault diagnosis in nuclear power plants (NPPs). However, current approaches often face challenges such as limited interpretability, data scarcity, and insufficient handling of open-set fault conditions. To address these issues, this article proposes a novel interpretable fault diagnosis framework that integrates graph-based representation with multi-task learning. The framework uses a graph structure to encode the physical and functional relationships within NPPs and integrates it with a hybrid network architecture for spatiotemporal feature extraction. Multi-task learning is then employed to simultaneously perform signal reconstruction, node-level anomaly detection, graph-level fault classification, and prototype learning. Experiments on two reactor systems show that the proposed framework achieves 100% accuracy in closed-set fault classification, even with limited samples, and outperforms baseline models. It also successfully identifies unknown and compound faults in open-set scenarios, providing interpretable insights into fault propagation and affected regions. These results illustrate the framework’s practical potential for improving diagnostic reliability and supporting operators in NPPs.

title: FBSTFnet: A full-band spatiotemporal fusion network for machine remaining useful life prediction
abstract: Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction is central to prognostics and health management (PHM) systems, enabling proactive maintenance and preventing major machinery failures. Current deep learning approaches often employ squeeze-and-excitation mechanisms for multi-sensor signal processing, but mainly capture low-frequency features and neglect important information in other frequency bands. In addition, existing spatiotemporal fusion methods rely on computationally heavy architectures that restrict practical deployment. To address these challenges, a Full-Band Spatiotemporal Fusion Network (FBSTFnet) is proposed, featuring four main innovations: a Full-Band Local Interaction Feature (FBLIF) mechanism that enhances multi-frequency representation through discrete cosine transform (DCT)-based spectral transformation; a hybrid architecture integrating gated recurrent units (GRU) with one-dimensional convolutions for efficient temporal–spatial feature extraction; an Easy-ProbSparse self-attention (EPSA) block that improves spatiotemporal fusion while reducing computational cost; and a Memory-Enhanced Local Feature Compensation (MELFC) block that restores long-term temporal continuity by reinforcing memory and compensating local features. The effectiveness of FBSTFnet is demonstrated on two benchmark datasets. Results show that FBSTFnet achieves a lightweight structure with accurate RUL prediction, providing a promising direction for advancing PHM in mechanical systems.

title: Bayesian adaptive elastic net for early prediction of battery cycle life
abstract: Accurate prognosis of battery remaining useful life is essential for evaluating reliability and optimizing the utilization of energy storage systems. To address the challenge of multicollinearity among degradation features, we propose a Bayesian adaptive elastic net method that improves prediction accuracy while providing comprehensive uncertainty quantification. The proposed approach implements adaptive shrinkage, applying separate penalty parameters to each regression coefficient to shrink the non-significant variables while preserving the effects of important predictors. By representing Laplace priors as Gaussian-exponential mixtures through data augmentation techniques and approximating the normalizing constant numerically, we develop an efficient Metropolis-Hastings-within-Gibbs sampling framework for posterior inference. Validation using numerical simulations and battery cycle life data demonstrates that the proposed method delivers superior prediction accuracy and robust uncertainty quantification, even under severe multicollinearity, providing an effective solution for battery lifetime prediction.

title: CSIR-Net: a continuous spatio-temporal information redundancy network based on structural priors for satellite telemetry data reliability enhancement
abstract: Enhancing satellite telemetry reliability is essential for status assessment and operational management. However, telemetry data have complex spatio-temporal dependencies and diverse missing patterns, making it challenging for traditional methods with discrete modeling, fixed parameters, and static prediction steps to recover. To address these, this paper proposes a continuous spatio-temporal information redundancy network that transforms degraded discrete data recovery into timestamp-aware continuous-trajectory inference with uncertainty-calibrated selection. Specifically, a long short-term memory network is reconstructed using neural stochastic differential equations to model hidden-state evolution in continuous time, and Ito integrals are incorporated to characterize uneven observation gaps, thereby enabling recovery at arbitrary timestamps. Additionally, time-varying signals and Brownian perturbations are integrated into the model to allow dynamic adjustment of parameters with the input, thereby improving the ability to recover multiple evolving features. Finally, a structure-prior-guided hierarchical graph is constructed to fuse multi-scale dependencies while suppressing redundant error propagation, and multi-head graph attention is used to derive adaptive confidence intervals for selective recovery, thereby improving telemetry reliability without obscuring novel patterns. Experiments on five datasets show the proposed method improves recovery accuracy by 27.7% over the best baseline, achieves 15.2–78.5 ms batch latency, and has strong potential for real-time large-scale telemetry reliability.

title: Lifetime Early Prediction for Second-Life Lithium-Ion Battery: A Hierarchical Bayesian Learning Method
abstract: With the rapid growth of electric vehicle (EV) adoption, the widespread use of lithium-ion batteries has brought increasing attention to the echelon utilization of second-life batteries (SLBs). These SLBs, typically retired from EVs upon reaching 80% of their rated capacity, possess considerable potential for deployment in stationary energy storage systems. To fully exploit their remaining capacity, accurate lifetime prediction during second-life applications is essential. This study addresses the early lifetime prediction of SLBs by proposing a hierarchical Bayesian model (HBM). Considering the heterogeneity in degradation behavior under varying working conditions, the method initially performs clustering based on operating conditions. Subsequently, a two-level hierarchical Bayesian framework is constructed to model the relationships between battery groups and individual units, enabling more accurate lifetime estimation. Bayesian inference is employed to optimize model parameters using extracted features, thereby reducing predictive uncertainty and enhancing overall accuracy. Validation on a self-collected SLB aging dataset demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms conventional machine learning approaches, especially under data-limited conditions. Quantitatively, the model achieves an average root mean square error (RMSE) of 113.444 cycles (±31.423), mean absolute error (MAE) of 76.616 cycles (±15.516), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 17.188% (±4.073%) on the test set.

title: PAKP: Parallelized Adaptive Kriging method with Partial least squares for high-dimensional reliability analysis
abstract: In structural reliability analysis, tackling high-dimensional problems with computational efficiency remains a significant challenge. To address this, the paper proposes a novel active learning method, termed Parallelized Adaptive Kriging with Partial least squares (PAKP), which is designed to enhance both accuracy and efficiency in high-dimensional reliability analysis of complex engineering structures. PAKP combines Kriging-based surrogate modeling with Partial Least Squares (PLS) for dimensionality reduction, effectively mitigating the challenges posed by curse of dimensionality. Another key innovation is the learning function allocation scheme, which adaptively selects the most suitable learning function from a portfolio to identify informative samples for refining the surrogate model. Additionally, a parallelization strategy is introduced to select multiple samples in each iteration, significantly enhancing the computational efficiency. An importance sampling scheme is also incorporated to handle small failure probabilities in high-dimensional settings. The effectiveness of PAKP is validated through five numerical examples, demonstrating its superior performance in balancing accuracy and efficiency. This highlights its potential as a promising solution for high-dimensional reliability analysis.

title: Cavitation reliability assessment of aviation fuel centrifugal pumps combining kriging and subset simulation important sampling
abstract: Cavitation in aviation fuel centrifugal pumps can lead to impeller erosion and performance degradation, posing significant reliability risks. To efficiently assess low-probability cavitation failures under multidimensional uncertainty, this study proposes a surrogate-based reliability analysis framework named AK-IEI-SSIS, which integrates Kriging modeling, an Improved Expected Improvement (IEI) learning function, and Subset Simulation Importance Sampling (SSIS). The framework adaptively refines sampling near failure boundaries to enhance accuracy and computational efficiency. Its performance is validated through multiple benchmark cases involving nonlinear and high-dimensional systems. A Python-based parametric platform is also developed to orchestrate parametric modeling, meshing, CFD simulation, and reliability analysis. Applied to an aviation fuel centrifugal pump, the framework accurately quantifies cavitation-induced failure probabilities as low as 5.63 × 10⁻⁴ using only 202 CFD evaluations, achieving a 99 % reduction in computational cost compared to Monte Carlo methods. Although demonstrated on a specific pump, the framework is applicable to reliability assessment of rotating fluid machinery under uncertainty, supporting reliability analysis and maintenance planning for next-generation aerospace propulsion systems.

title: Multi-fidelity Kriging structural reliability analysis with the fusion of non-hierarchical low-fidelity models
abstract: Adaptive Kriging is a common Bayesian statistical method and has founded wide application in structural reliability analysis. Multi-fidelity (MF) Kriging model can significantly reduce computational cost compared to single-fidelity Kriging model. However, research on MF Kriging reliability analysis remains relatively limited in the literature. Most existing MF Kriging approaches assume that reliability performance functions of varying fidelity levels follow a hierarchical nature, which is not applicable when the performance functions exhibit non-hierarchical fidelity levels across the input space. To handle this challenge, we develop a novel Bayesian adaptive MF Kriging method to integrate high-fidelity (HF) data with non-hierarchical low-fidelity (LF) Kriging models for reliability analysis. We first use the local correlation and variance-weighted fusion approach to fuse all the non-hierarchical LF models. Then, the hierarchical Kriging is employed for the construction of MF model based on HF data and the fused LF model. A new adaptive hierarchical refinement strategy is proposed. This strategy mainly involves a new hierarchical expected feasibility function (HEFF) for identifying the location and fidelity of the optimal sample simultaneously, and a low-fidelity-selection (LFS) algorithm based on Kriging-Believer approach to allocate simulations among non-hierarchical LF models. One numerical example and two engineering examples involving an aircraft tubing and an airfoil stiffener rib, are used to validate the performance of our method.

title: Causal graph inference with adaptive dynamic structure learning for mechanism-oriented fault diagnosis in dynamic industrial systems
abstract: Complex rotating machinery is essential to safety-critical industrial systems, where undetected faults may trigger cascading failures and pose serious safety risks. Inherent dynamic couplings, multi-source interferences, and time-varying feedback loops lead to complex fault propagation, presenting major challenges for reliable and interpretable diagnostics. Traditional data-driven methods, primarily relying on correlation-based models, often fail to generalize under non-stationary conditions and provide limited understanding of underlying failure mechanisms. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes the Dynamic Causal Mechanism Learning Diagnostics Framework (DCMLDF), designed to enhance system reliability and mitigate fault risks. The framework incorporates a multi-scale temporal encoder, semantics-aware causal graph inference, a causality-guided predictive decoder, and a unified optimization strategy to enable end-to-end modeling of dynamic fault evolution from high-dimensional sensor data. Evaluated on four benchmark datasets, DCMLDF consistently outperforms five representative baselines in both accuracy and stability. More importantly, it reveals system-level causal dependencies that characterize evolving failure pathways, thereby enabling early warning, root-cause identification, and risk-informed decision-making. These findings highlight the framework’s effectiveness in improving predictive reliability and operational safety, offering a scalable solution for prognostics and health management in complex mechanical systems.

title: Sparse Bayesian learning for joint load-parameter-response identification
abstract: The joint identification of the structural loads, parameters, and responses from the sparse measurements is crucial but challenging for assessing the operational conditions of civil infrastructures. Existing joint identification methods typically require the prior information, such as the loading locations and the covariance matrices of the process and observation noise, which are unavailable in practice. To address this limitation, a sparse Bayesian learning technique based on the transmissibility matrix is proposed for the joint load-parameter-response identification.
